title: Telemetry Management with Pipelines
subtitle: Treat the telemetry pipeline as a service
summary: Pip’s telemetry exports successfully but describes old conditions. Pipeline stages control reception, buffering, transformation, and delivery. Each stage can alter the evidence; visible backlog, age, and loss policies help the crew tell recovery from delayed ingestion.

concepts.title: Components separate responsibilities
concepts.body: Pip separates the telemetry path into receiver, buffer, processor, and exporter. One accepts, one holds, one transforms, and one sends. Chaining or combining those responsibilities creates explicit flow and routing controls. Pip avoids making every market application implement every destination’s format and delivery behavior.

concepts.title: Buffers absorb temporary disruption
concepts.body: Pip’s backend outage fills a local telemetry buffer. The queue or disk can preserve data temporarily and replay after recovery. If input persistently exceeds output, finite capacity eventually runs out. Pip treats buffering as time to act, not a replacement for throughput and overload policies.

concepts.title: Transformation changes evidence
concepts.body: Pip’s timestamp filter silently removes valid recent spans. Normalization, redaction, enrichment, and filtering change what downstream investigators can ask and trust. A healthy delivery rate does not establish correct evidence. Pip validates schemas, timestamps, and retained context alongside export availability.

concepts.title: Freshness and history can compete
concepts.body: Pip’s log storm leaves the dashboard hours behind. Processing all history first can hide current failure or recovery. Pip prioritizes fresh evidence when useful and handles backfill later if capacity permits. Visible policies and monitoring of age, loss, and backlog explain what a quiet graph actually means.

misconceptions.claim: A queue solves sustained telemetry overload.
misconceptions.correction: Finite buffering only delays exhaustion when input continues to exceed processing capacity.
Records can arrive with wrong fields, timestamps, or filtering; correctness needs end-to-end validation.

scenario.title: The application recovered, the graph did not
scenario.context: A telemetry backlog keeps showing old errors after a service fix.

options.label: Measure event age and prioritize fresh ingestion
options.benefit: Lets responders distinguish current behavior from delayed history.
options.cost: Requires explicit backlog and backfill policy.
options.consequence: Responders can assess recovery now while keeping backlog work visible.

options.label: Continue interpreting arrival-time graphs as current state
options.cost: Can falsely suggest the intervention failed.
options.consequence: Old failures may be mistaken for current failures and prompt unnecessary intervention.

scenario.debrief: Separate when work happened from when its telemetry arrived before drawing a recovery conclusion.

quiz.question: Input remains twice the export capacity for hours. What happens to a finite queue?
options: The buffer reaches a stable size as long as export remains available
Replay alone removes the mismatch without changing input or output capacity
Its backlog grows until capacity or policy intervenes
quiz.explanation: Buffers absorb temporary mismatch, not unlimited sustained overload.

quiz.question: After a pipeline rule change, export succeeds but one tenant disappears. What should be checked?
options: Filtering and transformation correctness across the pipeline
quiz.explanation: A successful transport can still deliver an incomplete or corrupted population.

quiz.question: Why might fresh events be prioritized during a backlog?
options: The oldest records cannot contribute to later incident analysis
Responders need current behavior to judge ongoing impact and mitigation
Freshness priority guarantees historical backfill will catch up at the same throughput
quiz.explanation: Freshness supports live response; historical processing can remain separate work.
